30 There is an electric current in a copper wire.
Which statement describing the average drift speed of the charge carriers in the wire is correct?
m s–1.
A
It is nearly 3  108
B
It is proportional to the cross-sectional area of the wire.
C
It is proportional to the length of the wire.
D
It is proportional to the magnitude of the current.

hints: Notice the question asks for the slow average drift speed $v$ of electrons through copper, not the fast speed at which the current signal travels along the wire.
Recall the current equation $I = nAvq$, where $n$ is number density, $A$ is cross-sectional area, $v$ is drift speed and $q$ is carrier charge.
Rearrange to $v = I/(nAq)$ for the same copper wire and decide which of current, area or length makes $v$ increase in direct proportion.
walkthrough: Identify the charge carriers as free electrons in copper with number density $n$ and charge $q$, moving with average drift speed $v$ through area $A$.
State the governing relation $I = nAvq$, so $v = I/(nAq)$ where $n$, $A$ and $q$ are fixed for a given wire.
Check the size: typical $v$ is of order $10^{-4}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ because electrons collide frequently, so nearly $3 \times 10^{8}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ confuses drift speed with signal speed.
Check geometry: $A$ is in the denominator, so $v$ is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and length $l$ does not appear at all.
Since $n$, $A$ and $q$ are constant, $v = [1/(nAq)] \times I$ shows $v$ increases directly with $I$. This is option D.

A.explanation: Drift speed in copper is typically about $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$, not nearly $3 \times 10^{8}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ which is the speed of an electromagnetic signal.

B.explanation: From $I = nAvq$, $v = I/(nAq)$ so for fixed $I$ a larger area $A$ gives a smaller drift speed - $v$ is inversely proportional to $A$.

C.explanation: The length of the wire does not appear in $I = nAvq$, so changing length alone does not change $v$ for the same current and wire material.

D.explanation: From $I = nAvq$, $v = I/(nAq)$ with $n$, $A$ and $q$ constant, so $v$ is directly proportional to $I$.
